content: Cooperation, or cooperative behaviors, refers to actions performed by organisms that provide benefits to other members of the same species. Several theories attempt to explain why natural selection favors certain types of cooperative behavior. It is important to note that more than one of these theories may contribute to the underlying reasons for the selection of such behaviors. Kin Selection One widely accepted explanation for the occurrence of cooperative behaviors is the theory of kin selection. This theory posits that individuals engage in cooperative actions to assist others who are genetically similar to them. By doing so, the genes responsible for such cooperative behaviors are preserved, as they contribute to the survival and reproduction of related individuals who share those genes. A classic example of this is observed in social insects like bees and ants. Worker insects, which do not reproduce themselves, dedicate their efforts to supporting the reproduction of the queen, who is genetically similar to them. Reciprocity The theory of reciprocity suggests that individuals perform cooperative behaviors because they receive something in return. For such behaviors to be evolutionarily advantageous, there must be a mechanism to ensure that the other individual recognizes and reciprocates the cooperation. Without this recognition, there would be no selective pressure to maintain the behavior. Much of the research on reciprocity as a driver of cooperation has focused on the prisoner's dilemma, a concept derived from game theory. Market Effect The market effect theory, proposed by Noë and Hammerstein, describes a mechanism that could lead to the evolution of cooperation. This theory is based on the idea that in many situations, there is a trade-off between the efficiency of obtaining a desired resource and the quantity of resources one can actively acquire. In such cases, partners in a system can benefit by specializing in the production of one specific resource and trading for another resource. For example, when only two partners exist, each can specialize in producing one resource and trade for the other. This trading process requires cooperation and involves negotiation and bargaining. The market effect can apply both within a species or social group and across species systems. It can also extend to multi-partner systems, where the owner of a resource has the ability to choose its cooperation partner. This model is evident in natural systems, such as interactions among apes or cleaner fish, and is also exemplified in international trade. For instance, Arabic countries possess vast oil reserves but require technologies from Western countries, which in turn need access to Arab oil. Cooperation through trade becomes the solution. Multi-Level Selection The theory of multi-level selection proposes that natural selection operates at multiple levels, such as the molecular and cellular levels within an organism, the organismal level, the community level, and even the species level. Any level that fails to compete effectively with others of the same level will be eliminated, even if the lower levels are highly competitive. A classic example is the role of genes that prevent cancer. Cancer cells divide uncontrollably and are highly competitive at the cellular level, as they reproduce rapidly and outcompete other cells in the body. However, at the organismal level, cancer is often fatal, which can prevent reproduction. Consequently, genetic changes that prevent cancer—such as mechanisms causing damaged cells to self-destruct—are favored by natural selection. Multi-level selection theory suggests that similar dynamics can drive individuals to cooperate in ways that avoid behaviors benefiting them in the short term but harming the community (and their descendants) in the long term.
